TITLE: The boring Bitcoin DCA rule I keep coming back to

BODY:
A few years into buying Bitcoin, the hardest part has not been understanding wallets, exchanges, or even volatility. The hardest part has been leaving the plan alone.

That sounds almost too simple, but it is where most of the damage happens. You start with a clean dollar-cost averaging plan, then a sharp move up makes you want to buy more, a sharp move down makes you want to wait, and suddenly the plan is no longer a plan. It is just market timing with a recurring-buy label on it.

I have made that mistake. More than once.

## The rule is boring on purpose

The rule I keep coming back to is this: choose the amount, choose the schedule, and only review the plan on a fixed date.

Not after a big candle. Not after a scary headline. Not because someone on social media is suddenly convinced the cycle is over. A fixed date.

For example, a monthly review works much better than a daily emotional check-in. You can still ask sensible questions: is the amount still affordable, is the exchange setup working, should withdrawals go to cold storage sooner, are fees reasonable? But you are asking them when you are calm, not when the chart is trying to negotiate with your nervous system.

That is the whole point of Bitcoin DCA. It is not magic. It is a way to remove the need to be brilliant at exactly the moment when most people are least clear-headed.

## Automation helps because discipline is finite

I used to think automation was just convenience. Now I think it is closer to risk management.

If the buy is manual, every purchase becomes a tiny decision. Should I buy now? Should I wait until tomorrow? Should I double this one because price dropped? Those questions feel productive, but most of the time they just reopen the door to emotion.

This is one reason I built [a free tool to automate Bitcoin DCA](https://btc-dca.com). The goal was not to create another trading bot. It was to make the boring plan easier to follow: connect an exchange, set the recurring buy, and optionally withdraw to your own wallet once a threshold is reached.

The less often I have to touch the process, the less often I can sabotage it.

## The part people skip: withdrawals

A recurring buy is only half the system. The other half is custody.

Leaving small amounts on an exchange for a short time may be practical. Leaving a growing long-term stack there indefinitely is a different decision. If your DCA plan is meant to run for years, then the withdrawal rule deserves as much attention as the buy rule.

My preference is to set a threshold: once the balance reaches a certain amount, move it to a hardware wallet. Not every day, because fees matter. Not never, because counterparty risk matters too. Somewhere boring in the middle.

Obviously I am not your financial advisor. You should choose your own risk limits and understand what you are doing before moving funds. But I do think a DCA plan without a custody plan is incomplete.

## What I measure now

I used to measure whether DCA was working by checking the portfolio value too often. That is a terrible feedback loop, because Bitcoin can make a good process look bad for months and a bad process look genius for a week.

Now I care more about process metrics:

- Did the scheduled buys happen?
- Did I stay within an amount I can actually afford?
- Did withdrawals happen according to the rule?
- Did I avoid changing the plan because of price noise?

Those are boring questions. That is why they are useful.

The strange thing about Bitcoin DCA is that the boring version is usually the serious version. Not because it maximizes every possible return, but because it is the version you might actually keep doing when the market gets loud.
